html:
Silla was a Korean kingdom in the southeast of the peninsula, from 57 BCE to 935 CE, one of the longest-lived states in Korean history. Its capital was Gyeongju.

It began as a small chiefdom and was long the weakest of the Three Kingdoms. It grew by absorbing its neighbours:

  • 527: Silla made Buddhism its state religion, after the martyrdom of the official Ichadon, according to tradition.
  • 562: it conquered the last states of the Gaya confederacy.
  • 600s: it allied with Tang China. Together they destroyed Paekche in 660 and Goguryeo in 668.
  • 670 to 676: Silla then fought its ally and drove the Tang out of most of the peninsula.

The result was Unified Silla, which ruled most of Korea while Balhae held the north. Society was ranked by the strict bone-rank system, which fixed what offices a family could hold. Silla had three reigning queens, including Queen Seondeok, and its elite youth trained in the hwarang corps. Gyeongju filled with Buddhist art; the temple of Bulguksa and the Seokguram grotto date from the 700s.

In the 800s nobles fought over the throne and peasants revolted. The kingdom split in the Later Three Kingdoms period, and its last king surrendered to Goryeo in 935.
sum: Silla was a Korean kingdom in the southeast of the peninsula, from 57 BCE to 935 CE, one of the longest-lived states in Korean history. Its capital was Gyeongju.
